job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Nikhil Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a rented room in a three-bedroom flat in Krakow with two friends, Tomek and Basia, who both found jobs already. Mornings I code for two hours on an open-source library for reading bank statements, with an AI assistant open beside me. Then I send applications and write to people on professional networks. In the evening I cook for the flat, which is my contribution to the rent war. I finished computer science with a data focus seven months ago.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was your final project, and what did the internships involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My thesis was a fraud-detection model for a credit union, and I got the top mark. I did one internship in the data team of a bank, cleaning data and writing dashboards, and one at a logistics software firm, where I fixed bugs in route planning. I like the practical side, where you build something and see if it works. I've had four interviews, all promising, and no offer yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a relief, but I wouldn't be shocked. I use the tools every day and they're handy, not magical. Better autocomplete, quicker boilerplate, but I still make the decisions. I'd tell friends to keep learning and not overthink the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be calm about AI but a little restless about my own timing. Four interviews with no offer isn't a catastrophe, but it makes me double-check my approach. I think the market is just choosy right now, and a plateau doesn't change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, about six a week, and I'd pick two open-source projects to make bigger contributions, because maintainers notice. I'd ask the logistics firm if they have a graduate opening. I'd also do small paid tasks on a freelance site to keep sharp and earn a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little itch to start. It's a decent world to begin a career in, and I'd feel lucky to have strong savings and a flat of friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your daily coding already uses AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What did you change after those four interviews?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomek and Basia, who already have jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I started practising the live coding questions with a friend, and I added a short write-up for each project in my portfolio. One interviewer told me that my code was good but I couldn't explain why I made choices. So I now record myself explaining my work, which is awkward but useful.

say: I'd say it's a relief, and tools are **handy, not magical**.
I'd tell friends to keep learning and not **overthink** the hype.
think: I'm calm about AI but a little **restless** about my own timing.
The market is simply **choosy**, and a plateau doesn't change that.
do: Make bigger contributions to two **open-source** projects.
Do small paid tasks on a **freelance** site.
feel: **Calm**, with a little itch to start, and lucky to have savings.

steps.text: Send six applications a week to Krakow and remote firms
Do paid freelance fixes on a task site
Record myself explaining my code choices each week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good time to be curious. Companies will need people who can direct the tools, and I'd tell friends to try them every day. I'd also say let's be honest: some entry jobs will shrink, and not everyone adapts at the same speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel a mild squeeze, but I'm well placed. I already use AI for most of my day, and I build things with it. The real risk is that firms hire fewer juniors and want people with experience that I don't have yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd target firms that are building AI-based products, because they need juniors who understand how the tools work. I'd put a project on my portfolio that was mostly built with agents, and write about the problems I found. I'd also apply to the bank's data team, where I interned, since they know me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slightly uneasy and excited. It's like the start of a new game, where the rules aren't yet written. I'd feel more tension for the friends who haven't tried the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you place yourself, compared with other juniors, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be near the front. I've used agents for coding since my second year, and I've broken them enough times to know their limits. That counts for something, but it doesn't guarantee an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change in your approach to the job hunt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add more product thinking, like asking what the customer really needs. When code gets cheaper, the part that stays valuable is deciding what to build. I'd say that to a hiring manager directly.

I'd admit some **entry jobs** will shrink.
think: I'd feel a mild **squeeze**, but I'm well placed because I already use AI most of my day.
The real risk is firms wanting **experience** I don't have yet.

Apply to the **bank's data team** where I interned.
feel: Slightly **uneasy** and excited, like a new game without written rules.

steps.text: Build a portfolio project with coding agents and write up the failures
Apply to AI product teams at Krakow software firms
Ask the bank data team about a graduate opening

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and nobody is ready. I'd say it publicly, plainly. Governments and firms need plans now, and workers should have a say. I'd also say that panic isn't a strategy, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be anxious. My skills are exactly the ones that machines do best, and two years is not enough to build a long track record. I'm better placed than most in knowing the tools, but when the tools can do the whole job, that edge shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast into the first job I can get, preferably in a team building these systems, so I learn what's coming. I'd save most of my pay, because I'd want a big cushion. I'd also pick up a hands-on skill, like electronics, as a backup, since robots come later. And I'd keep contributing to open source, because reputation might last longer than a CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. A mix of adrenaline and dread. I'd keep checking the news, which I know is a bad habit. But I'd feel less helpless than people who've never used these tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. Where does a junior data person fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd be worried, my mother especially, since she works at a bank branch and sees how it's changing. I'd say I have savings, I know the tools, and I'm acting. I'd also ask what they'd do if their jobs changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents, who live outside Krakow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the honest thing: nobody knows exactly. I'd show them I have a plan with steps. A plan with steps calms a worried parent more than a bold promise.

I'd add that **panic** isn't a strategy.

feel: **Unsettled**: adrenaline and dread, but less helpless than people who never used the tools.

fieldNote: He knows his tool skill is a **wasting edge**.

steps.text: Accept the first job offer on a team building AI systems
Save 60 percent of every pay cheque for a big cushion
Learn basic electronics through evening workshops
Talk through a plan with my parents and my sister

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a manageable timeline if people take it seriously. I'd tell friends to build useful skills, not just credentials. I'd also say that governments should pay for retraining while they still have budgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy but optimistic. I could have a first job, a second one, and real seniority by 2031. That might not be enough to stay ahead of full AGI, but it gives me options like starting a small firm with friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a job at an AI-heavy firm, learn on the job, and save a lot. I'd also start a side project with Tomek, who is good at hardware, around automation for small shops. And I'd probably go for a part-time master's in machine learning if my employer helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly. I'd still feel pressure, but it would be like a deadline I can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two years doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a bit less, around forty percent. With five years, I could take some risks. I'd put some money into a small business, and maybe a bit into index funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be saving that hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One thing it gives is the chance to turn skill into ownership. Working for someone else in this world feels fragile, but owning a tiny product that automates real work feels sturdier.

I'd tell friends to build useful skills, not just **credentials**.
think: I'd be uneasy but **optimistic**, with two jobs of experience by 2031.
That gives me options like starting a **small firm** with friends.

Start a side project on **automation** for small shops with Tomek.
Study part-time **machine learning** if my employer helps.
feel: **Hopeful**, mostly, with a deadline I can plan for.
S3.quote: Working for someone else in this world feels fragile, but owning a tiny product that automates real work feels sturdier.
fieldNote: Time moves him from **wage worker** to maker.

steps.text: Take a first job at an AI-heavy firm in Krakow
Build an automation tool for small shops with Tomek
Apply for a part-time master's in machine learning
Put some savings into index funds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great time to be young, if people are prepared. I'd tell friends to use the decade to try things, not to hide. I'd say it publicly and stay optimistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be calm. By 33 I could have a company, or a senior role, or both. Ten years is long enough to learn from failures, and I'm good at picking up new tools. I'd feel fine about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work, save, start a small company, probably with friends, and use the tools heavily. I'd build a few products, see what sticks, and keep the costs low. I'd buy a small flat in Krakow around 28 if prices allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite good, honestly. It's the one scenario where I'd feel excited, because it's the future I could design.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what are you trying to build?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairness, more than my own job. If a few firms own everything the tools produce, then the rest of us end up renting from them. I'd want rules that share the gains, even though I like building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still keep you awake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also worry for people who can't adapt as fast. Tomek's father drives a delivery van, and he's near fifty. Ten years is long enough for him to prepare, but only if someone helps.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because it leaves no space to build a record. What would help is a first job where I learn, public rules that share the gains, and honest advice from people who already work with these tools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Being comfortable with the tools doesn't make me comfortable with the future. I use AI every day, and I still can't tell you how this ends. I'd like people to know that it's possible to be both excited and scared.

headlineQuote: Being comfortable with the tools doesn't make me comfortable with the future.
portrait: Nikhil is **23**, a data-focused computer science graduate in Krakow, sharing a flat with two friends.
He uses AI **every day**, contributes to open source and treats interview feedback as homework.
His mood moves with time: calm in slow worlds, **anxious** when AGI is two years away.
He trusts building and ownership, and worries about **fairness** and slower adapters.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture, because there would be no space to build a track record.
whatWouldHelp: A first job where he learns, public rules that **share gains** and honest advice from tool users.
